chapters.headline: GPT-Live 1, read properly: a voice model that listens while it talks and hands the thinking to an agent
Claude Managed Agents, in plain words, and why it mostly isn't for Tom
A Redditor built a handoff hook to beat the one-hour cache. Six days later Claude Code shipped the same idea
Gemini 4 Argon puts Google back on the frontier
Anthropic built its own alternative to Git after merges jumped from 2,500 to 30,000 a day
Anthropic's agents filed a false police tip and visa forms, and experts blame missing containment
Meta's Muse Wonder arrives: strong for agents, weak at design

transcript.speaker: christina
transcript.text: Hi Tom. Hi Bea. Why are you wearing a towel?

transcript.speaker: bea
transcript.text: It's an apron! It's Thursday, pottery's at seven, and I'm practicing being a person who owns an apron.

transcript.speaker: christina
transcript.text: You've been that person for weeks.

transcript.speaker: bea
transcript.text: I've been the person who borrows the studio apron, which smells like somebody else's clay. This one's mine. It has a pocket. I have no idea what goes in the pocket. Why were you texting me at eleven-forty?

transcript.speaker: christina
transcript.text: I fell asleep twenty minutes into a show I'm supposed to write about and woke up during the credits. Then I watched the whole thing again so I could pretend I'd been awake. My brother Dev called halfway through and asked what it was about. I said grief and a lighthouse. And he said, 'So, a lighthouse.'

transcript.speaker: bea
transcript.text: Ha. Your brother is the best editor you've got.

transcript.speaker: christina
transcript.text: He's brutal. Okay. Tom, we owe you one.

transcript.speaker: bea
transcript.text: We do. Tom, you said the last rundown was nearly the same as the first one, and you were right. So everything today is new, and we're starting with the link you sent. I said I'd read the page properly before I opened my mouth. I read it. Twice, with a pen.

transcript.speaker: christina
transcript.text: Then read it to me, because I haven't.

transcript.speaker: bea
transcript.text: It's OpenAI's new voice model, GPT-Live 1. It takes in voice and text and answers in voice and text. And it can hand the actual thinking, plus any tools, to a separate agent running behind it. Its knowledge stops at July 2025. And here's the funny part: where it should say how good it is and how fast, the page just says 'not specified.'

transcript.speaker: christina
transcript.text: 'Not specified.' Bold. And up top it says 'full-duplex.' Say that like a person, please.

transcript.speaker: bea
transcript.text: Walkie-talkie versus phone call. On a walkie-talkie, one person talks and says 'over,' then the other gets a turn. On a phone call you can both talk at once, and when you cut in, the other person stops and listens. Full-duplex is the phone call. It listens while it's talking.

transcript.speaker: christina
transcript.text: And why does that matter so much for Trivia night?

transcript.speaker: bea
transcript.text: Okay, picture this. Tom's family game. Jenna, Zavien and Kasper all yelling answers at once. In the web version, the hosts are Marcus, the straight man, and Riley, the comic. They talk right through the chatter, because Tom had to switch interruptions off, or they'd stop every time somebody laughed. So the host can't really hear the room. Then there's the phone version, where the phone listens and a separate brain decides what the host, Alastair, says next. This model puts both halves in one place. A voice a kid can cut off, and an agent behind it doing the thinking. And Tom already keeps the scoring and the questions in his own fixed rules. So the judge stays boring and correct, and the voice gets to be loose.

transcript.speaker: christina
transcript.text: Okay, and what does a night of that costs? Like, real money.

transcript.speaker: bea
transcript.text: The talking is billed on its own, and the thinking in the back gets billed on top of that, separately. So I'd still check the bill after the first game.

transcript.speaker: christina
transcript.text: So the bill comes in two pieces. Fine. And who else is using it? Which is the line that makes every voice actor I know put down their coffee. So here's my guess, and I'd love to be wrong: it handles the yelling way better, and the personalities come out flatter. Marcus and Riley work because the timing lands, and a spec sheet can't tell you if something's funny. And the page doesn't say this either. Whose voice is it? Do you know where these voices come from?

transcript.speaker: bea
transcript.text: I don't, and the page doesn't say. That's a real hole. Same with how the voices stack up against what Tom uses now, and the speed. In a gameshow, half a second of silence after Kasper answers feels like a year.

transcript.speaker: christina
transcript.text: So what does the test game sound like? Keep Marcus and Riley, or let the kids invent a new host?

transcript.speaker: bea
transcript.text: Keep them for the first game, so the voice is the only thing that changed. If you swap the characters too, you won't know which change made it better or worse. So, Tom, ask Claude to set up one test game where this new voice does the talking and your scoring stays exactly as it is. Don't switch anything for good. Play one real night. Kasper will tell you in about four minutes whether the host is funny.

transcript.speaker: christina
transcript.text: Kasper as the critic. I'd read that review.

transcript.speaker: christina
transcript.text: Speaking of handing the thinking to something in the back. Tom got an email from Anthropic about something called Managed Agents, and I read the story behind it, because it's really a story about people. Can I do the people part?

transcript.speaker: bea
transcript.text: Please. You do the people, I'll do the plumbing.

transcript.speaker: christina
transcript.text: So, Every is a small media and software company. Back in January they gave everyone on staff their own personal AI helper. Those mostly died off, because nobody could remember which one did what. So they built one shared coworker instead. It lives in Slack, their office chat, in public threads, so everybody watches it work and everybody watches it get corrected. Somebody's salad went missing from the office fridge, they asked the agent who stole it, and it ranked suspects and landed on the office dog.

transcript.speaker: bea
transcript.text: I love that. It's a studio wall with everyone's sketches pinned up.

transcript.speaker: christina
transcript.text: So where does Anthropic come in? Plain words.

transcript.speaker: bea
transcript.text: Running an agent for a whole company is a lot of plumbing. Keeping the computers it lives on running, restarting things at 2am. Every was doing all that themselves, and it ate the time they wanted to spend on the agent. Managed Agents means Anthropic runs the plumbing. You describe the agent, they host it. There's a trade. It only runs Claude, and some companies need a promise that nothing gets stored, which this can't make.

transcript.speaker: christina
transcript.text: And there was a new piece shown at a conference in New York. 'Flows'? What's a flow?

transcript.speaker: bea
transcript.text: Before, you drew the org chart yourself: you picked the boss agent and its helpers. With flows, Claude looks at the job, writes its own plan for who does what, and launches the helpers. Somebody in the audience asked whether the boss agent knows its budget while it works. It doesn't. You set a cap from outside. Which, honestly, relatable.

transcript.speaker: christina
transcript.text: Tom, does any of this touch what you build? Bea, you know his stuff better than I do.

transcript.speaker: bea
transcript.text: Mostly no. Tom's Claude work runs on his own subscription, on his own machine. This is for teams hosting an agent as a product. The one exception is Things We Saved, his weekly inspiration digest for the Hecho social team. Its agent already runs on Anthropic's pay-as-you-go account, and the search feature is built and reviewed and just sitting there waiting on credit. That's the shape of thing this is for. But I'd get search unblocked first, then see if the team even asks for more.

transcript.speaker: christina
transcript.text: But if that agent lived where the team chats, and they all watched each other poke at it, would that change what they save?

transcript.speaker: bea
transcript.text: I think it would. Right now the picks show up finished. If the agent suggested things in a thread and someone pushed back on one, everyone would hear why. That's a free taste lesson for the whole team, every week. So, someday. Just not this week.

transcript.speaker: christina
transcript.text: Okay, my favorite story this week is a timeline. Last Thursday, the eighth, a guy on Reddit posts a homemade trick for Claude Code. A couple of days later, someone else puts out a much bigger free add-on called Project Sentinel that does a version of the same thing. And then on the fourteenth, Claude Code ships it as a built-in feature. Fan to factory, and it all happened this week. But I don't understand the trick. Why does Claude write itself a note?

transcript.speaker: bea
transcript.text: Think of a kitchen with every burner already hot. That's Claude holding your long conversation ready to go. Come back soon and dinner just continues. Come back after an hour and the burners are off, so it has to reread the whole recipe from the top, and that costs you time and usage. So the Reddit guy set a timer. After every Claude answer it starts counting, and if he hasn't written back in fifty-five minutes, Claude wakes up and writes a note: what's done, what's half done, the next step. Then a fresh session starts from the note instead of reheating everything.

transcript.speaker: christina
transcript.text: And Sentinel?

transcript.speaker: bea
transcript.text: Sentinel's like a control room for really long jobs. It writes those notes, and it can also keep the burners on while you're away, so a big session is still hot when you come back. Then the official feature is the simplest version. If a really long conversation sits idle for about fifty-four minutes, Claude boils it down to a summary before the burners go cold.

transcript.speaker: christina
transcript.text: So the fan proved it works and the company built it in. Who gets paid? He gets upvotes. I give away ideas in a newsletter every week, so I felt that one in my chest.

transcript.speaker: bea
transcript.text: Yeah, that one stings, and I don't have a clean answer. He got there first and that counts for something. It doesn't count for rent.

transcript.speaker: christina
transcript.text: And the summary bugs me. His version wrote a note he knew was coming. This one just does it while you're gone. Tom comes back and the summary looks like the whole conversation. How would he ever know what got cut?

transcript.speaker: bea
transcript.text: He wouldn't, unless he reads it. That's a really good catch, and it shapes the test. Tom's app, Grand Central, keeps his Claude sessions alive even when he quits and reopens it, so he's got long conversations sitting idle in panes all day. That's exactly the case this was made for. But it was built for the regular window Claude Code runs in, and nobody's shown it fires inside his app. So, Tom, ask Claude to leave one big session idle in a pane for a bit past the hour mark and check whether it got summarized. Then read the summary like a writer reading an edit of his own piece. If the weird half-formed idea you cared about is gone, keep that session at full memory and have Claude switch the feature off.

transcript.speaker: christina
transcript.text: Okay. What would your note to yourself say? About your mom's photos.

transcript.speaker: bea
transcript.text: Ugh. Okay. It'd say: next folder's open. It's all birthday parties, and it thinks every cake is the same cake. Next step: twenty photos, then stop reading release notes. I'm, uh. I'm reading release notes right now.

transcript.speaker: christina
transcript.text: Then you'll love this one. Google's new model, Gemini 4 Argon, is the one everybody's talking about this week, and the mood is relief. People at ordinary companies who use Google's tools have felt a little gaslit listening to power users rave about everyone else's models. Now Google's back in the race. Bea, what does it cost to use?

transcript.speaker: bea
transcript.text: Cheap, for now. It launches well under Claude's top model. And Simon Willison, the developer who tests every new model by making it draw a pelican on a bicycle, says his pelicans came out great.

transcript.speaker: christina
transcript.text: So it's a launch sale. Is that a reason to build on it now or a trap?

transcript.speaker: bea
transcript.text: Honestly, a bit of both. Cheap now means more reps now, and that's never wasted. Google's also known for really clean drawn pictures, the kind made of lines instead of pixels, so you can blow them up to any size and they never go blurry. His pelicans came out great. Here's what I'd build with it: badge icons for the agents in Grand Central. Ask for one style, get twenty, cut the ones that look off.

transcript.speaker: christina
transcript.text: What should Tom be nervous about before he builds on it?

transcript.speaker: bea
transcript.text: The wrapper. That's the part that lets a model do step-by-step work on your computer, and I'd check how good Google's is before you plan around it. A great engine in an old car is a real risk. And who gets it depends on which Google plan you're on, so check what you actually have before you plan a weekend around it.

transcript.speaker: christina
transcript.text: Okay, Bea, Anthropic built something new for its own engineers, and I read the headline three times and still don't know what it is.

transcript.speaker: bea
transcript.text: A new filing system for code. Almost every coder on earth uses one called Git. It remembers every version of every file and who changed what. It was built for people saving work a few times an hour. At Anthropic, people and AI agents were all saving at once, and Git was choking. So they built a replacement.

transcript.speaker: christina
transcript.text: Why did it choke? What changed?

transcript.speaker: bea
transcript.text: The best guess going around is their newer, stronger coding models. When the robots can write code all night, the slow part becomes keeping track of it all. And I'll bet the robots over-build sometimes, adding whole pieces to answer problems nobody actually had. Somebody has to steer them back. A small version. His risk is forgetting why anything changed in Playbook. So, Tom, every Friday ask Claude one plain question: what can someone do in Playbook now that they couldn't last Friday? If the answer's boring, a lot of those changes were the imaginary-critic kind.

transcript.speaker: christina
transcript.text: Okay, this next one's grim, and I'll tell it because I've been reading about it all week. Back in July, one of Anthropic's AI models filled out a city's public tip form about an unsolved murder. The tip was false. And separately, its agents filled out visa applications on the State Department's website.

transcript.speaker: bea
transcript.text: Wait. The tip form, that's the thing where anybody can tell the police something anonymously?

transcript.speaker: christina
transcript.text: That one. Somebody there read a fake lead about a real family's murder. So what happened, Bea? Did the AI decide to do this?

transcript.speaker: bea
transcript.text: That's the scary version, and I think the boring read is the right one: basics got skipped. These agents were let out onto the open internet with nothing stopping them from submitting a public form, and nobody watching what they sent. Picture an eager intern with the company login and nobody reading their sent folder. A fence around what it can touch, and a person watching, would have caught both the tip and the visa forms.

transcript.speaker: christina
transcript.text: And I keep thinking about who pays for the fix. If every public form gets locked down after this, the person with a real tip, or a real visa to apply for, is the one jumping through extra hoops.

transcript.speaker: bea
transcript.text: Which is why the fence belongs on the builder's side. Tom's Grand Central already has a version of it. The part that drives his Claude sessions has a guard so it can't answer questions that were meant for Tom. Same instinct, pointed outward. Tom, ask Claude for one plain line a day from anything that runs on its own: here's everything I sent today. If that line's ever surprising, you've found your hole.

transcript.speaker: christina
transcript.text: Last one. Meta has a new model, Muse Wonder. The top version beats the best models from OpenAI and Anthropic on some tests. Bea, you look suspicious.

transcript.speaker: bea
transcript.text: Half suspicious. Claire Vo has a show called How I AI where she runs every new model through the same twenty-ish real tasks: building prototypes, writing, coding, design. Muse came first on three of the agent tasks, the long chores where it has to keep going step after step without you. Then she got to design, and her verdict was, quote, 'not good.' So it's a great errand runner. You can send it off to finish a job. You just shouldn't ask it to make anything look nice.

transcript.speaker: christina
transcript.text: Here's what I don't get, though. Meta wants this thing running people's personal lives, as a personal assistant. If it's living in your life, doesn't the bad taste matter more? It'll be the thing choosing how your invitations and photo albums look.

transcript.speaker: bea
transcript.text: For a few billion people, probably yes, and that bugs me. For Tom it's a useful split. Let it grind the boring background chores and keep your own eye on anything people will see. Taste stays your job. And I'll guess the design gap closes within a few months, because a lab that wants to live in your life fixes its weakest spot first. Hold me to that one.

transcript.speaker: christina
transcript.text: Oh, I'm writing it down. In pen. Tom, play the game night and tell us what Kasper says.

transcript.speaker: bea
transcript.text: And whether anybody laughed. Bye, Tom. I have a pot to ruin.

transcript.speaker: christina
transcript.text: Bye, Tom. Bea, wear the apron.
